originalTitle: Australia politics live: Andrew Bragg says low-income earners should accept they will live in substandard housing; David McBride granted parole
content: Telstra CEO gets $6.8m after 20% bonus cut over outage Telstra has paid its chief executive, Vicki Brady, $6.8m for the year ending in June, after docking 20% of her bonus in response to the network’s nationwide outage last month. The company reported financial results today and said its board decided to cut Brady’s bonus by $607,000 when it met on Monday. Brady took home $6.1m the year before, so she still got a $700,000 pay rise. The company has faced heavy political criticism for its handling of the outage, which it has blamed on the lack of a software update on a key time-keeping system. Telstra also docked 20% of the bonus for its former networks group executive and 10% of all other senior executives, the equivalent of $1.3m unpaid. The company’s results show senior executives were paid $20.7m combined for the year. The company reported its profits rose to $2.4bn, from $2.3bn the prior year. It paid shareholders a dividend of 21 cents per share over the year. The strong result was helped by job cuts, with employee numbers falling 1,219 to total 29,334 by June. It was also helped by steep price rises: income from mobile phones rose $300m, with customers paying an extra 7.2% on prepaid handheld plans and an extra 3.4% on postpaid handheld plans. Despite the rising prices, Telstra sold 1m more mobile plans, and now has 26m services in operation. Catholic Schools NSW CEO to appear before Icac The Catholic Schools NSW CEO, Dallas McInerney, will appear before the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) when it resumes its hearings at 10am this morning. As part of its investigation into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberal party, Icac is investigating whether illegal donations were made by the governing body for 600 schools in the state, arranged and approved by McInerney, to support the alleged branch stacking efforts of conservative Christian group the Reformers. The inquiry has repeatedly heard a message sent by McInerney, who is a factional ally of federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, to a Reformer advising of a plan to “shake down Angus for 10K”. Taylor has not been named in Icac’s allegations and has repeatedly denied he ever made payments to the Reformers. Tasmania must be prepared for ‘risk of mass mortality event’ after bird flu detected Tasmania’s environment minister, Guy Barnett, said the community “must be prepared for the risk of a mass mortality event”. He said Tasmania had worked closely with the federal government to develop protection plans for the most at-risk species including the critically endangered orange-bellied parrot, the Tasmanian devil, the shy albatross, the short-tailed shearwater, the Furneaux white-fronted tern, the fairy and little tern, Australian and long-nosed fur seal, and the Australasian gannet. Barnett said as soon as the state received approval it would begin vaccinating up to 350 captive orange-bellied parrots: We’ve been working with the commonwealth to get approval to vaccinate our orange-bellied parrots, and I’m very pleased that we’re now very close to being able to commence that work ahead of our scheduled release of birds to the wild. He said the captive facility at Five Mile beach was central to the national breeding program and already operated under strict biosecurity arrangements. Additional protective measures, including specialised shade cloth infrastructure, are being implemented to reduce the risk of disease transmission from wild birds to captive parrots. Victorian premier’s message to students ahead of walkout protesting against Pauline Hanson: ‘Stay in school’ At the end of his press conference, Victorian premier Ben Carroll was asked about the national student protests against One Nation and Pauline Hanson. Thousands of school students will attend protests around the country today, including in Melbourne, Sydney, Perth, Canberra, Adelaide, Brisbane, Newcastle and Wollongong. Carroll said: First and foremost, my message to every student is: if you want to change the world, stay at school, focus on what your learning is in the classroom. I understand they’re angry with the sentiment and the policies of One Nation, but the best way to change your future in the world is to get an education and to stay in school. ‘We should learn from the mistakes from the past’: Albanese Anthony Albanese says the bailout comes back to jobs and sovereign capability, hammering in the point of Australia not being at the end of supply chains. This is pretty front of mind at the moment, with the world having experienced multiple supply chain crunches due to global conflict in recent years. He brings up the death of the car manufacturing industry and the closure of oil refineries in Australia as mistakes from the past that governments should learn from. The fact that oil refineries shut in this country under the former government that now we’re having to go out there and look at how do we become more sovereign. How do we become more resilient? And the idea that we would sit back and watch this facility just disappear is not in Australia’s national interest. This will produce a return to Australia. This is connected up with an increasing clean energy, which will drive this change through. It’s connected up with not just the jobs that are created directly here, but their indirect jobs that will flow through the manufacturing sector right throughout this country. David McBride is being released from prison in Canberra this morning. He has served his full non-parole period of 27 months. In May 2024, the former army lawyer was sentenced to a maximum five years and eight months in jail for his role in stealing secret defence documents about the Afghanistan war and leaking them to the media. McBride pleaded guilty to three charges in November after the court upheld a commonwealth intervention to withhold key evidence the government argued had the potential to jeopardise “the security and defence of Australia”. chineseContent: Telstra首席执行官因停电而削减20%奖金后获得680万美元 Telstra在截至6月份的财年中向其首席执行官Vicki Brady支付了680万美元，此前该公司因网络上个月在全国范围内出现停电而削减了她20%的奖金。该公司今天公布了财务业绩，并表示董事会在周一开会时决定将布雷迪的奖金削减 607,000 美元。布雷迪前一年拿了 610 万美元，所以她仍然获得了 70 万美元的加薪。该公司因其对停电的处理而面临严厉的政治批评，该公司将其归咎于关键计时系统缺乏软件更新。 Telstra 还扣留了其前网络集团高管 20% 的奖金和所有其他高级管理人员 10% 的奖金，相当于未支付的 130 万美元。该公司的业绩显示，高级管理人员今年的薪酬合计为 2070 万美元。该公司公布利润从上一年的 23 亿美元增至 24 亿美元。该公司全年向股东支付每股 21 美分的股息。这一强劲业绩得益于裁员，截至 6 月份，员工总数减少 1,219 人，总数为 29,334 人。它还得益于价格的大幅上涨：移动电话收入增加了 3 亿美元，客户为预付费手持设备计划额外支付 7.2%，为后付费手持设备计划额外支付 3.4%。尽管价格不断上涨，澳洲电信还是多销售了 100 万个移动套餐，目前运营中的服务数量已达 2600 万个。新南威尔士州天主教学校首席执行官将出席新南威尔士州反腐败独立委员会 (Icac) 今天上午 10 点恢复听证会的新南威尔士州天主教学校首席执行官达拉斯·麦金纳尼 (Dallas McInerney)。作为新南威尔士州自由党涉嫌腐败调查的一部分，廉政公署正在调查该州的管理机构是否为该州 600 所学校提供、安排和批准非法捐款。
